reason: The orbiting debris needs to gather where Earth's tides will not tear a forming Moon apart.
expectation: Debris beyond the disruption region will be able to collect into a Moon-forming body.

effect: The debris must first collide and spread into a ring; I can now try the region beyond tidal disruption.
reaction: I was wrong about the first step, but the collisions explain how the debris redistributes.
reason: Material in the spreading ring may gather into a Moon beyond the region where tides disrupt it.
expectation: Some of the spreading rock will move beyond the tidal disruption region, where it can begin to gather.

effect: The spreading ring produced growing moonlets beyond the disruptive tidal region; they still need to gather and cool.
reaction: It is satisfying to see why the location matters for clumps to survive.
reason: Gravity can pull the growing moonlets together into a larger body.
expectation: The moonlets will merge into a growing Moon.

effect: The moonlets have gathered into a hot young Moon, which still needs to cool.
reaction: The assembly worked as expected; the extensive melting is a useful detail.
reason: Escaping radiation can carry heat away from the young Moon and allow a crust to form.
expectation: The Moon will cool and begin forming a crust.

effect: Cooling produced crystals in the lunar magma ocean, but the crustal-raft goal remains unfinished.
reaction: The distinction between crystallization and crust formation is useful.
reason: The crystals may form a crust as they separate within the Moon’s magma ocean.

choice.combine: Crystals in the lunar magma ocean

expectation: Some crystals will gather into a lunar crust.

effect: Buoyant crystals formed a feldspar-rich layer; it may still need to cool into a crust.
reaction: The role of mineral buoyancy in building the crust is interesting.
reason: Escaping radiation may cool and solidify the floating layer into lunar crust.
expectation: The floating layer will cool into a lunar crust.

effect: The floating layer cooled into an early lunar crust, completing the Moon goal. The inward-falling debris still needs to return to Earth.
reaction: The pale crust forming before the familiar dark maria is a useful distinction.
reason: Earth’s gravity may draw the inward-spreading debris back toward the planet.
expectation: Some debris will fall inward toward Earth.

effect: The inward-moving debris is now falling back toward Earth; it still needs to reach the surviving planet.
reaction: The split between Moon-forming debris and returning rock is clear.
reason: The falling rock should return its material to the surviving Earth.
expectation: The debris will rejoin Earth, completing the remaining goal.

effect: The falling debris rejoined Earth, adding heat and reworking the planet; both chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The return path makes the impact debris feel consequential for Earth as well as the Moon.

mostWorthwhile.text: Forming the lunar crust was most worthwhile: cooling, crystallization, and buoyant feldspar made a useful physical sequence rather than an instant transformation.

leastWorthwhile.text: The final return to Earth was straightforward once the debris was already falling inward, though it completed the story.

surprise.text: I was surprised that relatively buoyant plagioclase could help build the Moon’s pale early crust.

arbitrary.text: My initial attempt to move debris beyond the tidal disruption region felt premature in retrospect; the feedback explained that collisions first redistribute it. No action stood out as purposeless.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the chapter connected satisfying assembly with understandable physical processes, and I would be curious to see how the remade Earth develops.
